Languid

/LANG-gwid/ - the stress falls on LANG · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Languid means sluggish from fatigue or weakness.

Jet lag left the whole crew languid, drifting through the soundcheck a half beat behind the drummer.

Worked Example

By the last mile of the charity walk, Grandad's stride had gone languid—each step a small negotiation—so we claimed the shady bench and let the finish line wait.

Languid is more exact than 'tired' because it describes how the tiredness moves: slow, heavy-limbed, drained of push. Sleepy people want a bed; languid people are still going, just at half power.

How Languid Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

listless

listless: flat from lost interest more than lost strength

sluggish

sluggish: slow to start and slow to move, like cold syrup

Antonyms

energetic

lively

lively: quick, bright, and animated

How Strong Is It? — relaxed → languid → exhausted

relaxed vs. languid

relaxed vs. languid: Relaxed is the pleasant, milder state—muscles loose by choice, energy still on call the moment it's wanted.

exhausted vs. languid

exhausted vs. languid: Exhausted goes further than relaxed—an exhausted hiker has nothing left at all, while a languid one still drifts forward at half speed.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — langu

Root — langu: to droop, be faint (Latin languere)

Suffix — -id

Suffix — -id: in a state of

Put it together

Put it together: Langu- (to droop, from Latin languere) + -id (in a state of) = in a drooping state. The same -id caps torpid and placid in this unit: Latin's way of turning a condition into an adjective—languid, drooping; torpid, numbed; placid, calmed.

Use the root in a new word: languish

Use the root in a new word: languish: Add -ish and the drooping stretches into a state: the appeal languished in the clerk's inbox for two years, growing no closer to a ruling.

Root Check

Word Choice

literary / descriptive

Languid is for weakness you can watch: heavy limbs, drifting pace, a wave that barely lifts. Its unit-mates carve the territory finely—torpid is a deeper shutdown, closer to dormancy; somnolent is specifically sleepy; and listless (a chip above) is flatness of interest rather than of strength. If nothing is wrong and the slowness is delicious, 'lazy afternoon' may serve better than languid.
